newsitem.title: ITALY: U.S. praises Italy for "job well done" in Albania.
newsitem.headline: U.S. praises Italy for "job well done" in Albania.

text.p: The United States on Monday praised Italy for doing a good job in leading a security force in Albania that helped key elections pass off in relative calm.

"I would like to express my appreciation for the extremely important role Italy has played in helping Albania to hold successful parliamentary elections," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright wrote to Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.
Her letter was released after Italy announced that the 7,000 troops of the 11-nation mission it leads would withdraw by August 12.

"The success of the effort thus far owes much to the outstanding leadership shown by Italy in helping to organise the Multinational Protection Force and in providing strong support to the OSCE," Albright said.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) monitored the elections in which the ex-communist Socialist Party scored a landslide victory. OSCE envoy Franz Vranitzky conducted months of shuttle diplomacy before the poll.

Albright noted some "troubling incidents" in the first stage of voting on June 29, and fresh violence was reported in Sunday's second round, but the poll passed off in relative peace in a country that has been under gun rule for months.

"The United States will maintain its own strong engagement on Albania and work through the OSCE to see that efforts to rebuild democratic institutions and a sound economy there remain on track," Albright told Dini.
"We look forward to working closely with you...Thank you once again for a job well done." The United States was not part of the mission, dubbed "Operation Alba".

Italy's Defence Chief of Staff Admiral Guido Venturoni, commander of the security force, said earlier the troop withdrawal would begin on July 20 and would end within 20 days "if there are no complications".
He told reporters at a book presentation he expected the troops to be "all out" by August 12.

Italy's centre-left government almost fell in April over resistance from its hard-left parliamentary ally to dispatching the force, the first such mission to be led by Italy. Venturoni said it had to overcome some difficulties, but had proved a success.
"The Multinational Protection Force has managed to restrict organised crime greatly, to keep open communication routes and to get the country moving again," he said.

The United Nations agreed a 45-day extension of the force's mandate on June 19 after its original term expired on June 28. The extension followed a request from Albania's national unity government, installed to restore political stability in the run-up to elections intended to end months of mayhem.
"We've worked miracles putting together a force with 11 countries, including countries with a strong military tradition such as France," Venturoni said.
"The French don't like being under anyone else's command if they can help it. We've managed to get Turks and Greeks to get along," he added.

With the elections over, Rome is trying to speed up the return of an influx of Albanian refugees granted temporary sanctuary in Italy by offering financial incentives and the possibility of qualifying for temporary work permits.

"For every repatriation, by August 31, a contribution of 300,000 lire ($176) has been set to ease reinsertion into Albania," Giulia Falzoi, an official of the Geneva-based International Organisation for Migration (IOM), which will oversee the repatriation, told reporters in Rome on Monday.
"Anyone deciding to return by July 31 will have 200,000 lire extra," she added.
